video_title: What happens on the day the president fears AI will kill him? | Jeremie Harris (x-post from NonZero)
transcript: Rob Wiblin: Hey listeners. Today we’re  crossposting an interview with Jeremie Harris   from the NonZero podcast hosted by Robert Wright.  I had somehow not heard of Jeremie Harris already,   but I found this a super thought-provoking  conversation. Jeremie just had a lot of   ideas that were new to me, especially regarding  warning shots and the likely government response,   and also possible mistakes that have been made in  AI governance in the past. It’s all debatable, and   I’m sure not everyone will remember the history  the way that he does — I’m not sure that I quite   remember the history the way that he does — but  I think it’s provocative in a really useful way. You might know the interviewer, Bob Wright  or Robert Wright, because he’s actually been   a guest on The 80,000 Hours Podcast before. He’s  also the author of a number of bestselling books,   perhaps most notably The Moral  Animal: Why We Are the Way We Are,   and he just published a new book about  the arrival of AGI called The God Test:   Artificial Intelligence and Our Coming  Cosmic Reckoning. If you’re somehow not   already convinced that the creation of  smarter-than-human machines is of cosmic   significance and will lead us to a new era in  the universe’s history, well, go read Bob’s book. Bob now also does very regular interviews  about AI and AGI and superintelligence — he   interviewed Nick Bostrom a couple of weeks ago,  for instance. One of Bob’s strongest and most   distinctive views is that if the US and China  can’t set aside their differences and coordinate   to manage the arrival of superintelligence,  then we’ll probably just be toast as a species.   You’ll hear him make some of the case  for that perspective in this interview. Anyway, I really appreciate Bob letting us  crosspost the conversation — especially the   second half, which was the highlight for  me, but has been completely stuck behind a   paywall until now. So thanks, Bob, and thanks,  Jeremie, and I hope you enjoy the crosspost. Robert Wright: I’m Robert Wright, publisher  of the Nonzero newsletter. This is the   Nonzero podcast. I’m also author of  the recently published book on AI,   The God Test. Excerpts are  available at thegodtest.net. And you are Jeremie Harris, and you  know a thing or two about AI. You are,   for starters, cohost of one of my  go-to AI podcasts, Last Week in AI,   cohosted with Andrey Kurenkov —  if that’s not too much mangling   of his name. And you are CEO and cofounder of  Gladstone AI, which in 2024 released a State   Department–commissioned report which I would  say, in retrospect, looks like it anticipated   some themes that are more prominent in the current  AI discourse. I’m sure you would say the same. Jeremie Harris: I’m sure I would. Robert Wright: I’m sure you would.  In fact, it may be that you have on   your podcast — I’m not sure, though.  But I was aware of it at the time,   and it was pretty much on my wavelength,  and that’s one reason I remember it. For one thing, there was the recognition  that national security in the age of AI   cannot be secured through policy at  the national level alone. Ultimately,   you’re going to need what has lately been called  international coordination. And the report does   emphasise that — has a particular plan for getting  there. It emphasises the kinds of risks that we’ve   been hearing about lately: bioweapons, cyber —  and the phrase “loss of control” is in there,   something that has become more prominent in  the discourse since the Hugging Face incident. So are you glad that regular  people have finally caught up   with your prescience? You  might not put it that way. Jeremie Harris: Well, I’ll accept  the framing begrudgingly, but yeah,   I think it’s clear that right now the idea  of rogue AI is now sort of widely accepted,   because it has to — because  we’ve literally seen it. So that report did come out in 2024, early 2024.  It was the product of research that started in   2023. Actually, the report itself was commissioned  by the State Department about a month before   ChatGPT — before the Eye of Sauron was on this  issue. Nobody in the US government was paying   attention to it, which meant that there was no  pressure to bureaucratise, let’s say, the output   of the work, the report itself. And so that’s  really the only reason that we were able to. And so there was this sort of funny situation  that unfolded where basically we’re revealed to   be working on this thing that suddenly became of  massive public interest in the immediate aftermath   of ChatGPT. But it’s too late for the government  to— there’s no takebacks. And so off we go,   writing this report that the government now  knows will one day be public. And there’s   all this kind of political back-and-forth,  because the administration at that time — it   was Biden — did not want terms like AGI to  be used in this thing, because it seemed like   science fiction. They didn’t want terms like  “loss of control” to be included. And so we   had a pretty intense political fight behind the  scenes to make those things appear in the report. We felt it was essential just because, as  you know, Silicon Valley has been talking   openly about artificial general intelligence  and superintelligence as being the end goal   of what they’re doing. I wouldn’t even call it  the worst-kept secret in Silicon Valley. It is   the open and stated primary objective of the  world’s most valuable companies at this point,   or many of them. And so anyway, we  just wanted that to become public. I think one of the things in retrospect that  it kicked off was it was, to my understanding,   the first time that there were published in  kind of mainstream outlets sort of insider   whistleblower reports from the frontier  labs themselves. And at that time it was   a lot riskier. One guy took me aside after a  meeting at one of the frontier lab headquarters,   and he just gave me his phone, and his  hand was shaking. He was like, “Hey,   can you put your number in my phone?” And what  he told me at the time actually was, “Whatever   your recommendations in this report are going to  be, I would urge you to please be more ambitious.” And later on, we met him literally at  a bar off site, just to kind of get the   rundown of what he meant by that. And  he was talking about nationalising the   frontier labs. This was 2023, he was  saying. We’re getting there, right? So I think this kind of crazy world — these  sort of almost science fiction scenarios,   or what seemed like science fiction then — is  now starting to just become mundane reality. The   Overton window has shifted so much that I think  it’s time to reassess a lot of these proposals. Robert Wright: Yeah. Let me say one thing in  anticipation of our conversation about where   you and I do and don’t overlap, because I think  this is what’s going to make this an interesting   conversation. As I’ve said, we both emphasise  the eventual need for something that I would call   international governance — you might or might not;  some people prefer other terms. But one difference   between us is I’ve heard you describe yourself as  a China hawk, and I’ve heard you talk like a China   hawk. I’ve heard me describe myself as definitely  not a China hawk. So it’ll be interesting to see   how we navigate some of these issues together,  and what we do and don’t agree on — on what’s   possible, first of all, and what’s necessary,  and what the implications of all this are. But yeah, back to the discourse. It has been kind  of shocking. I mean, it’s funny: so you wrote this   report before some of this stuff happened. I put  this book of mine, The God Test, to bed before   the breakout — the OpenAI breakout — and the  trajectories we’re seeing now unfold are in   the book. We already had Moltbook and various—  and I talked about agents, and I talk about loss   of control. In fact, I have a chapter called “Hive  Minds and the Loss of Control.” Although I didn’t   anticipate the specifics of this kind of scenario.  So I’ve had this weird feeling of like, “Wait, so   I’m prescient? Oh, wait, no, it’s too late to be  pre—” It’s like— the discourse is moving so fast. Robert Wright: And two things. First of all,  people in this realm have for some time been   saying, “Look, what’s it going to take to  get the world’s attention? I guess we’ll   need a warning shot” — by which they generally  mean some kind of high-casualty catastrophe. In that sense, the news is good. The Overton  window’s moved a lot, very low body count.   There have been tragedies involving AI, but  so far as I know, nobody died at Hugging Face.   And so that’s all good. But I’m wondering  what you think in terms of, first of all,   what is the discourse still not  catching up to, in your view? And   secondly, do you think it’s still  going to take more kind of jolting   incidents of some kind or another to get  the discourse to where you want it to be? Jeremie Harris: Yeah, I think these  are really complicated questions,   but I think, at least in my view,  they have a relatively simple answer.   The simple answer is there is still somehow  alpha in just taking scaling seriously. So scaling is this idea — I think by  now it’s sort of a household idea,   but just in case it isn’t — this idea that  if you want to make an AI system smarter,   all you have to do, roughly speaking, is train  it at a larger scale, with more computing power   and more data. So you take this model,  this artificial brain, right? And again,   you use more AI processors, more of these chips,  built in a bigger AI data centre with more power   and so on. And now we’re at the scale where we’re  doing this with gigawatt scale. A gigawatt is   like a million homes’ worth of power, right? So  these are truly mammoth facilities and sites. AI buildouts are responsible for the  lion’s share, if not basically all,   of US economic growth over the last  few quarters. So if you zoomed out,   you would see planet Earth is slowly  transforming itself — not so slowly,   even — into just a computing factory. And the  economy is sort of starting to reflect that,   the markets are starting to reflect that,  political pressures are starting to reflect   that. And yet the simple fact that scaling just  works is still something that, by believing it   more than others, you can still, I think, make  better predictions than the average person. Back in 2020, the first time that  my cofounder and brother Ed and   I bet big on this was when we left our  company in 2020. There was a paper that   came out around that time. It was  the first big scaling laws paper. Robert Wright: Was that a company you had  started? I’m just curious, what was it? Jeremie Harris: Yeah, so it was an experiment.  And this— maybe, I don’t know if this goes to our   differences necessarily, but this was a hardcore  experiment in libertarian economic theory. So— Robert Wright: Well, that would be one  difference, not necessarily related to the   China-hawkism issue. But yeah, I’m looking for  Milton Friedman on my bookshelf. Oh, not there. Jeremie Harris: Yeah, yeah, absolutely. And to be  clear, as we age, our views become more nuanced.   But this was sort of a fun experiment in how far  could you take that? And so it had this notion   of income share agreements, where you might get  educated at some school or whatever, get some   training, and then the training could be monetised  by taking a percentage of your salary for a   certain period of time, so you don’t have to pay  upfront. And nominally, incentives are aligned in   that way. It actually kind of became the world’s  largest marketplace for income share agreements. And we would do kind of peer to peer. So  if you wanted to break into, typically, AI   or data science, you’d work with a  mentor, and the mentor would say, “OK,   I’ll help you for free” — somebody who works  at Tesla or OpenAI — “in exchange for 3%,   5% of your first-year salary when you  get hired.” And so we had thousands and   thousands of these mentorships happening. It was  a really cool experiment, and we got some really   genuinely fascinating economic data from it  that is, I think, to this day quite unique. But the scaling laws paper came out, and I  still remember I had a two-hour conversation— Robert Wright: So this was Dario on  this paper? Yeah, when is this? And   this is establishing — arguing — that  yeah, all it takes is more compute,   more data. And that certainly has gotten us—  well, a lot of innovations have happened,   let’s face it. But that has partly driven what  we’ve seen. That was Dario’s name on that? Jeremie Harris: Yep, that’s right. So Dario was  involved in all the early scaling research. In   fact, he was kind of the champion of scaling.  It’s often said of OpenAI that they are really   scale-pilled, and they are, but there are  a lot of ways in which Anthropic actually   is much more aggressively scale-pilled than  OpenAI, in different ways. And a lot of that   comes down to Dario. He was the earliest believer  in it, really, along with Ilya in a lot of ways. Robert Wright: And he was at  OpenAI when they first showed   the benefits of scaling with the early ChatGPT. Jeremie Harris: That’s right, yeah. And so if  you talk to the OpenAI people — so Jack Clark   will tell you GPT-2 is kind of the  moment that he went, “Whoa, whoa, whoa.” And really, maybe it’s worth talking  about just what these things are scaling,   because it’s abstract to say you scale data,  you scale computing power or whatever. But   the actual thing that you’re scaling is  basically a text autocomplete engine.   And so all it does is it gets really good at  predicting the next word. It sounds stupid,   but text autocomplete ends up being, by  some weird freak of information theory,   this really important task. And you can  kind of understand why that’s the case. If I give you a sentence like, “To counter a  rising China, the United States should blank,”   right? In order to fill in that blank — in order  to fill it in accurately — you need to know what   the United States is, what China is, what it means  for China to be ascendant. You need to know facts   about geopolitics, economics, all kinds of crap  that goes into just filling in that one next word.   And so this turns out to be a really powerful  way of teaching AI models just about the world   generally: facts about physics, about how to code,  about how to orient yourself in the world. And so— Robert Wright: I mean, if I could add one thing. Jeremie Harris: Yeah. Robert Wright: You also need — if you’re going to  do that efficiently, and the process of training   forces the machine to do it efficiently — you need  a way of, for example, representing the meaning   of words. And I think it’s underappreciated—  something that the brain presumably does. I   think it’s underappreciated the extent to which  training is kind of the reverse engineering,   from language, of, I would say, some of the  cognitive functionality that in humans evolved   to help us deal with language. And then of course  there’s the subsequent so-called post-training,   where they do more than autocomplete: they teach  it to answer various kinds of questions and so on. And I think the reverse engineering continues,   and this is why the ‘stochastic parrots’ people  are just not getting the power of what’s going   on. Without having to understand how the human  mind works, we’re kind of reverse engineering   the rough equivalent of it. And all you need  is the right kind of data and a lot of scale. Jeremie Harris: Yeah, that’s right. And  the analogies and disanalogies are really   interesting here. There’s a sense in which it’s  really easy to get lost in the minutiae — the   Gary Marcus-ing of a lot of the conversation here  — where there’s always some fascinating reason   to believe that scaling will magically stop.  Perennially there is some fascinating argument:   we’re hitting a data wall, we’re hitting a  compute wall, we’re hitting an energy wall,   we’re hitting this wall, that wall.  Stochastic parrots, as you said, right? These arguments often wildly outlive— at least in  the discourse, they wildly outlive their utility   or their evidentiary foundation. We’re way past  stochastic parrots. I’m old enough to remember   when the data wall was supposed to be a reason  that you wouldn’t get offensive cyber capabilities   like Mythos. We just don’t seem to refactor our  kind of credibility index when we’re thinking,   “How seriously should I take a Gary Marcus?” Well,  maybe — or Yann LeCun — maybe we ought to look   back and see what predictions they’ve actually  made about the present moment before we go off. And the economic version of this too, which  kind of drives me up a wall a little bit,   is people who say, “Oh, well, this whole AI  thing is overhyped. There’s a massive bubble,   it’s going to pop. These aren’t real businesses.”  And while it could be a bubble that pops — and   I’ve heard you argue sort of similarly before  on the show; I think this is exactly right — it   could absolutely be a bubble that pops. It could,  independent of the trajectory of the technology,   for any number of reasons that are  mostly economic and not technological. But Anthropic has had its first profitable  quarters. If they want to, they can turn this   into a money machine. The race to scale right  now is about who owns more market share. That’s   the classic kind of VC financing model. And the  margins for these companies have been going up.   If you look at the margins for Anthropic right  now, they’re sitting increasingly in comfortable   software-as-a-service territory — like 70%  territory. OpenAI is headed that way too. And so   far from dropping— again, I’m old enough to  remember when the margins were supposed to drop,   everything was supposed to go dark.  This is the opposite of that trajectory. And consistently, everyone has been surprised  by how fast things have gone and not how   slowly. I say this with some modesty, because  I called it incorrectly in the other direction,   where I said— frankly, I thought  we ought to be dead by now,   based on my median estimate. So  what the hell do I know? But yeah,   that’s the shape of it as I see it. I think we’re  accelerating faster than most people appreciate. Robert Wright: Yeah, I’m going to add an asterisk  but not pursue it, because I want to get back   to where I initially derailed this by asking  you what your company was before you and your   brother moved on to your next venture. I will say  — and I hope we’ll get back to this, because it’s   relevant to the China question and whether you  can slow down without China catching up and so   on — that the challenge Anthropic does face is  staying ahead of the commoditisation, right? Jeremie Harris: Yes. Robert Wright: And the value of what  it’s doing now lies in the fact that,   clearly, its models are superior to much  cheaper models. And one question mark is:   can it sustain that indefinitely? If  not, what will plan B be? But anyway,   I’m sure you have things to say about that, but  I’m kind of feeling guilty about taking you off   your original path. We should return to the part  of your story, I guess, where your libertarian— One more asterisk: ironically, some  of your— I don’t want to say enemies,   but some people who drive you crazy  are libertarians, because they’re   still arguing that this technology needs  essentially no regulation. Another thing   maybe we’ll get back to. We will not name any  names. The name David Sacks will not come up. Jeremie Harris: No, but Marc Andreessen  will not be mentioned in this. Robert Wright: Will not be  mentioned. But let me take   you back to where you were. Continue your journey. Jeremie Harris: Well, yeah, so actually, I  guess we’ve covered part of it. This paper   comes out. Ed and I at the time are very happily  working away in this weird Milton Friedman–style   economic experiment. The paper comes out and  we have a sort of tense two-hour phone call,   and he gets the better of me. He’s basically like,  “Look, I’ve looked at this paper. The scaling laws   seem to be holding across— it’s like seven orders  of magnitude in computing power.” So basically,   if you train a model with 10 units of compute,  and then you train it with all the way up to   like 10 million units of compute, 100 million  units of compute, you just see this merciless,   ruthless, unending straight line that  will not bend. It will not yield. And this has a certain aesthetic to it.  If you think about how evolution worked:   for evolution to work, you need to  have a very smooth hill to climb,   right? If you’re going to work your way up  the intelligence ladder through evolution,   an increment of intelligence has to yield an  increment of reproductive fitness, right? And so   it had to be a simple thing. The brain had  to be something that was made up of simple   components that could gradually increase in  complexity over time, over generations. And   when you look at a scaling law like this,  the argument Ed was making was like, “Look,   of course nature would be shaped this way.  It had to be a scaling law of some kind.” We just seem to kind of have  unlocked it. Transformers,   which is the architecture of essentially  the artificial brains — the AI models we’re   scaling in this way — just seemed to have the  property that they were extremely resilient,   that these scaling curves would not yield.  And so this was enough for us to go. When GPT-3 came out, which was, gosh, like  what, two and a half years before ChatGPT,   we looked at that and we’re like, “Oh my God.”  Not only do we have these scaling curves,   but now for the first time we  have an AI that, bear in mind,   was not ever meant to be anything other than a  text autocomplete system. And yet it can code,   it can design basic websites, it can  translate between languages, it can do   all kinds of things it was never meant to do,  just by virtue of the scale of its training. You train it on enough internet text, enough  Wikipedia pages, enough textbooks — eventually,   if you give it a sentence like, “Below is  a piece of code that checks the weather,   colon,” it will know, like, “OK, well,  I’ve read a bunch of blog posts online   that have a description of a piece of code,  and below is the actual code. So I’ll just   write up that code.” It could do that. And so  immediately, to us, this implied we were on a   trajectory for human-level AI and beyond.  Immediately it implied that AI was about   to become the single most important source  of national security risk in human history. Jeremie Harris: This sounds crazy.  It sounded crazy then. We literally   started going around talking to  anyone who would listen in the US   government and other governments — UK,  Canadian — to try to wake people up. And one of the things that happened — and this is  something that I think is underappreciated about   the kind of AI safety ecosystem of the time  — there were a very small number of funders,   of grantors, in that ecosystem. The main one, the  mack daddy of the AI safety ecosystem at the time,   was Open Philanthropy — now Coefficient  Giving, but back then Open Phil. And they   were funded by Dustin Moskovitz,  one of the cofounders of Facebook,   and very kind of tied to the effective  altruist cause that has become so kind of   famous — infamous — nowadays, that maybe we can  get into. I think it’s an important part of this. But they had this view that if you  spoke to anybody in the government,   what would happen is that they would hear  you. If you came to them and said, “Look,   we’re on the cusp of building human-level  AI. We think we’ve cracked the code,   we think the scaling thing has legs. You may not  appreciate this, but Silicon Valley is talking   about this as if they have cracked the code, and  they’re investing exponentially more every year.   They smell blood right now. So this is about to  become a real national security problem. We do not   think we’ll be able to control the systems that we  build, and we will get rogue AI incidents in all   likelihood out of this. That may be challenging  for the human species at a civilisational level.” If you pitch that argument to somebody in  government, the Open Phil people argued at   the time, this would trigger a very specific  reaction. The US government guys would go,   “Oh wow, I hear you about the capabilities. That  sounds really compelling. It sounds like a really   powerful weapon. I’m going to ignore all the  warnings about the risk, and we’re going to   trigger a Manhattan Project for superintelligence”  — that only gets humanity killed faster. Now, this is a very specific— and it was  expressed, by the way, with extreme levels   of confidence. There was a paranoia at the time  about doing anything that wasn’t, as they put it,   “robustly good.” And everybody ran around  sort of almost worshipping at the altar of   a small number of folks at the top of the  pyramid, who were typically the grantors. And I think there’s a big psychological issue  there, where when you get used to doling out   money, you don’t realise that people start  to change their tune when they talk to you,   to align with your preexisting beliefs. And you  sort of fall into a well of your own making — kind   of surround yourself inadvertently. These are  good people, but they surrounded themselves,   I do think, with a lot of folks who kind  of reinforced their preexisting views. Robert Wright: So were they literally  trying to keep the government people   in Washington from knowing kind of almost  the central theme of their own discourse? Jeremie Harris: I think that’s a fair  description, with one little modification,   which is there was at the time— and this is  just my view. There’s nobody here from their   end to kind of give their explanation of it, so  I’ll try to be as sort of even-handed as I can,   but I am biased, of course. There was a small  number of folks at the top of that pyramid who   were ordained in some sense by the ecosystem  as those who were sort of responsible enough   to carry the message to government in their own  way and in their own time. Those individuals I   had many arguments with refused to, and strongly  discouraged us to, use the phrase “artificial   general intelligence.” They were part of— they  themselves were putting forward this argument. And the case that we were making at the time was  like, “Look, I get that you have this concern,   but right now artificial general intelligence  is not a thing that people know about. And so   you have an opportunity to get in here  and shape the battle space around that   terminology before it becomes politicised  — because it will. Anything that rises to   high enough levels of salience becomes  politicised. That’s just a fact of the   matter. And so this is an opportunity for you  to kind of inform folks who are actually going   to make decisions ahead of need.” And they  warned us against it. They actually said,   “Look, there’s also this whole kind of  principal–agent or prime mover risk,   where whoever is the most irresponsible will  do this first. Please don’t be that guy.” And so, last thing I’ll say about  this — and I think this kind of   again leans back into the libertarian  startup founder side of who we are,   which at our core is who we are — our  instinct in hearing this was like, “OK,   most startup ideas are terrible.” They feel really  good. We feel the truth of our ideas very deeply,   and they’re often just laughably wrong.  They do not survive contact with reality.   The kind of startup impulse is to say, well,  probably my product — and therefore almost   my identity, if I’m not careful — but really my  product is crap, and so I need to put it in front   of people as fast as possible in a low-stakes  setting, and then iterate as quickly as possible. And so we thought to ourselves, “OK, well, let’s  just start talking to people. Let’s see if this   thesis actually holds up. Let’s bother to just  talk to one person who clearly is not empowered   to do anything with this information.” And we  did. And by and large — much like if you look   at polls of the US population right now and you  ask people how they feel about superintelligence,   how they feel about rogue AI, they’re passing  the test with flying colours. They are correct.   Superintelligence is likely to be a massive risk  to human civilisation and people. The public’s   intuition on this is basically right — just like  US government officials’ positions on this were   basically right when they were first introduced to  it, at least by us, back in 2020, 2021, that era. And so just by doing this and iterating  on it, we very quickly found, like, “Wow,   this massive money cannon that these folks are  holding on to is just pointed at a thesis that   has not even been tested” — or at least that  failed our test, and that continued to fail as   we escalated the sort of rank and impact of the  folks that we were talking to. And so that for us   was a bit of a wake-up call as to one of these,  I think, deep pathologies, unfortunately, in the   ecosystem. It’s no longer, by the way, the view  of these entities, but it certainly was back then. Robert Wright: Yeah, no, I was going to  say, you were prescient in that sense too,   because they are now engaging in the  Washington discourse. But I’m wondering,   did they have a plan at that point as to  how they were going to kind of circumvent   normal channels of Washington  influence and yet save the world? I mean, it’s funny — I think maybe part of  the answer to your question is this vibe   you still get from people like Dario. Not maybe  explicitly, but you get the sense that they think,   “Well, if we just are the first ones to build  superintelligence, we will, through alignment   or some kind of—” I would say magical process,  somewhat dismissively, because I don’t think this   is going to do it. But through some such process,  as long as it’s a good guy who does it — as long   as it’s Dario and not Sam — then we’ll be OK.  Well, it was like a private sector— that’s a very   libertarian solution. We don’t need the government  at all. But was that what they were thinking? Jeremie Harris: Well, so, OK, this is a really  good and important and interesting question. I   think for one thing, I’ll just say we made the  choice once we started to see this pattern where   we were hearing really confident— and by the way,  these very confident calls they were making didn’t   just end at “Don’t talk to government, because  this will be the response.” They also included   just massive miscalculations on AI timelines,  and not necessarily— OK, so AI timelines and   also what you do about them. So I had many  arguments with folks in this ecosystem that,   like, “Look, scaling laws — I think this is the  trend that gets us there, to superintelligence.” And there was all this sort of speculation  at the time about— actually, who I’ll just   name: Ajeya Cotra, because I’m actually a huge  fan, and she’s over at METR now — was involved in— Robert Wright: She’s very impressive. Yeah. Jeremie Harris: Yeah, that’s right. Well,  at the time she kind of championed this Bio   Anchors framework, which was a way of thinking  about AI progress through the lens of, like,   well, here’s how much time — or how much  compute, I should say; how much effective   kind of computation — was involved in shaping the  human brain and kind of leading to evolutionary   intelligence. If you look at   the movements — who’s actually selling data to  whom, and how are frontier labs consuming that   data — there’s a Chinese footprint there, a  big one. I’m not just saying a one-off thing;   I mean things that matter at scale,  even for the behaviours of these models. It applies at the data centre layer. So if  you look at who’s building data centres in   the United States, often on suspiciously short  time horizons — being able to get access to   transformers in six months, when they should  be on three-year backorder, from China — their   level of penetration of the North American  tech stack is obscene, in a way that it just   isn’t reciprocally. And so from a human placement  standpoint, from a supply chain access standpoint,   China just enjoys advantages that we do  not have symmetrically. And we have a   lot of capability that we need to build up  to be able to get to parity on this stuff. Our one last best hope right now, the  big kind of equaliser, is cyber. And the   problem with cyber is increasingly there’s  this view— and we’re sceptical of aspects— Robert Wright: So we, in other  words, thanks perhaps to Mythos,   have superior cyber capability, you’re saying. Jeremie Harris: Right. Well, that’s right.  So nominally— so the CIA and the NSA have   really doubled and tripled down on cyber for  a whole bunch of reasons, some of which have   to do with risk appetite and not wanting to put  people out in the field as much, but also just   the leverage that comes from the technology. So  they’re really overleveraged on cyber right now,   and physical placement and access and supply chain  — these sorts of things that we need to kind of— Robert Wright: But it’s a  problematic kind of leverage. Yeah. Jeremie Harris: Exactly, exactly. China is in our  bones in a way that we are not in their bones.   And in terms of the collection ability, right —  so the ability to verify in informal ways that,   hey, is OpenAI letting it rip secretly and  running a big— well, let’s ask any one of   our dozens and dozens of people who are in  the lab, some of whom are explicitly spies,   but most of whom are just people we have  leverage over. Let’s just ask them. That’s   one option you have. You also have espionage in  terms of physical implants in the data centre,   supply chain attacks — all these things that they  can do that are much harder— I’m not saying we   don’t do them, but they’re a lot harder for us  to do, for all kinds of reasons, over in China. And so we need to get to parity. Cyber right  now is a really important lever that we have   that we’re relying on too much. And I say too  much because it’s entirely plausible that as AI   systems get better and better, they get better  at defence than at offence. So a given piece— Robert Wright: That’s not a consensus  view, right? But it is your view. Jeremie Harris: It’s— so we have another report  that we’ll be putting out on this. It has been   a semi-consensus view at Anthropic among some  of their security folks for a little while now,   just as they’ve seen trends. So the argument is  something like this: a given piece of software   will have finite complexity. There are only  so many ways that you can hack it or crack it.   So if you direct a sufficiently powerful  model or agent at that piece of software,   eventually you’ll buff out basically all the  vulnerabilities that actually do exist. Now,   this is fallible. I think it’s  a weaker argument than it seems,   in a whole bunch of ways that don’t  really matter for this discussion. But the point is that you actually could  enter a regime in which you actually do have   pretty surprisingly good cyber defence vs cyber  offence, where the kinds of vulnerabilities that   we find and look for get a lot harder to  find and look for in the kind of post-AI   world of just 18 months from now. If you do  that, suddenly offensive cyber operations   do not give us the leverage that we’re used  to. And we find ourselves in a world where,   from a cyber standpoint, we’ve got nothing  too special. China, though, has supply chain,   human — they’ve got physical access, all  kinds of things that we don’t have. And so   the ability to actually enforce, if China then  goes to try to renege on their commitments,   suddenly vanishes, and is seen by China to  vanish, which emboldens them to do more. And so there’s a sense in which the lack  of parity— this is one of my big issues   with Dan Hendrycks’s MAIM [Mutual  Assured AI Malfunction] framework:   I don’t think it accounts for the objective  situation on the ground as seen by a lot   of folks. I’m not aware of special—  like SAPs, special access programmes,   dark black programmes or whatever — that I’m  not aware of, obviously. But by and large,   from what I’ve seen and heard, it seems like this  is more or less the situation. And so I’m much   more concerned about US offensive parity than I  am about China’s ability to do things that would   knock our stuff out of the swim, say. Anyway,  that seems to me to be a really important element. Robert Wright: So I know you’ve got  to go in a few minutes, and there’s   two questions I’m dying to ask you, so I’m  afraid we’re going to have to cut to those. One is: I’m sure you’ve read the part of Dario’s  Machines of Loving Grace paper where he talks   about the need for a bloc of democracies  to beat a bloc of authoritarian countries,   obviously led by China, to superintelligence,  use that to— I think it’s fair to say he wants   to bring them to their knees.  But in any event, his demand,   as I recall — I think this is almost verbatim — is  to get China to “stop competing with democracies.” Now, first of all, I don’t know exactly what  he means by that. I’ve never heard anyone ask   him. Some people think he means regime change in  China; some people think he means something else.   So my first question is: do you have a sense for  what he means? And secondly, what is your view on   this overall question? Do you share what seems to  be one of his assumptions — that China does want   to impose a system of governance on us, and for  that reason alone, the race to superintelligence,   if we can’t avoid it, is existential? Of course,  in your view, it’s existential either way,   because we’re toast if the planet gets there. But  if you could tell me what you think his view is,   and then what your related view is on  China’s kind of foreign policy aspirations. Jeremie Harris: Yeah, so my answer, in a  weird way, comes from the same uncertainty   in both cases. I don’t know what Dario—  so I’ve met Dario, talked to him one time,   two or three years ago or something,  right? So it was an hour-long conversation,   and that’s about it. I don’t know where his head  is at, and the specific meaning of the words. Generally, the threat model I’ve just laid  out here is certainly one in which you don’t   need to frame things in quite the way that  Dario has. It’s in the self-interest of the   Chinese and the Americans to do this, right? But  that self-interest is, in my view, insufficient   to kind of cause everybody to hold to their ends  of the bargain here. America needs more offensive   heft and the willingness to deploy that. And  yes, it needs verification tech and so on. I think a bloc of aligned powers is actually  really important for the West from a supply   chain standpoint. It gives us just more  leverage. I would rather the West end up with   much more leverage than the Chinese. I’d rather  approximately the situation be reversed. Right   now — one thing we didn’t talk about is robotics,  and the massive advantage that the Chinese have if   you just let things play out status quo right now.  If you look at the dark factories that the Chinese   are spinning up, the scale at which they’re just  pumping out robots, humanoid robots — everybody   talks about the ageing Chinese population. Forget  it. Not going to be an issue. This is just— Robert Wright: It may be an  issue for them domestically,   in terms of— the jobs issue may be  an issue for both. But go ahead. Jeremie Harris: If they can  subsidise universal basic income,   or true total luxury communism or whatever,  through this sort of thing. Yeah. Anyway. So in terms of whether we need that bloc, I  think the scenario as I see it is you need,   first and foremost, verification from that first  moment. Of course, verification using satellite   telemetry and various other collection options  that the national security apparatus already   has vetted and available to it, and that it  institutionally knows how to process and trust.   You’re going to kind of start to back  into more and more fine-grained tech,   and that is more and more permissive as we  get more and more resolution and more access. And as we do trust building— I will say,  historically, the Chinese response when   American diplomats say, “We need trust-building  measures,” the Chinese response is to say,   “Oh, we can’t do that, because we don’t  trust you.” This is literally how they— Robert Wright: But they believe that, and  we feel the same way about them, right? Jeremie Harris: Right. But the trust-building  measures — the purpose of them is explicitly   to get us to that next level of trust. So there  is this sense in which the adversarial dynamic,   at least in ways that are intelligible to us—  and I think to your point, this is important:   we are interpreting it as meaning that  they are not engaging in good faith in   that way. It is possible — and reasonably  likely, of course — that there’s a story   they’re telling themselves about how the  situation is quite the opposite. But yeah. So a bloc of aligned countries, I think, is really  good insofar as it gives us leverage. By the way,   I think nonkinetic, noncyber options are  really the first thing we need to look   for. There are ways, when you talk to some of  the supply chain people, of doing one-shot,   six-month slowdowns of China’s, for example,  chip ecosystem, where you only can use it once,   but you can use that card for a six-month  slowdown. So the kind of thing that could be   fairly punitive and reasonably nonescalatory.  But you want that wider range of optionality.   It helps you across that spectrum to have a bloc  of allied countries. And I think certainly more   engagement with the Five Eyes and NATO would  not be a bad thing for the US at this point. Robert Wright: And you agree that the alignment  should be explicitly ideological? In other words,   in Dario’s view, these are democracies. So I  guess even if Russia just begged to be on board,   and they— whatever, we’d say, “No, sorry,  your elections are phoney.” I personally   think there’s real danger in casting the  narrative that way. I think it tends to   become a self-fulfilling prophecy of a  bipolar, ideologically opposed world.   But is it your view that ideology should be  a big part of the litmus test for inclusion? Jeremie Harris: I’m fairly ambivalent, honestly  — probably because I haven’t thought enough   about it. Like anyone, my reflex would be I  want the democracies to win. But zooming out,   there’s just no winning to be had in a  superintelligence loss of control race.   And so I think it’s really just about trust — and  not even about trust, but our ability to verify.   So if we have a country like France, where, as  you said, our friendliness to France just means   that we have all kinds of ways of monitoring  what’s going on there that we don’t have with   Russia — yeah, to me that’s just an extra  tick in the verification box for France. And it happens to be that a lot of the countries  for which we enjoy that level of closeness,   we have that relationship because they  are pluralistic liberal democracies   and all those wonderful things. But as a  counterpoint to, I guess, Dario’s framing,   it’s not obvious to me that Russia gleefully  jumps into bed with China on this one. North   Korea is in a fraught relationship with the  Chinese and the Russians. These are not coherent   ideological blocs. I mean, socialism with Chinese  characteristics — the second part of that phrase— Robert Wright: Is not socialism. Jeremie Harris: Right. And just as Russia is— Robert Wright: Well, and Russia— I mean, look,  I wish people would quit calling China— I mean,   a communist country. It is run by a party called  the Communist Party. But anyway, go ahead. Jeremie Harris: Yeah, exactly. In much the  same way as Russia is a sort of vaguely   fascist-flavoured authoritarianism with  religious overtones. I don’t know what   term is right for these things. And the beauty  is, on my worldview, I don’t particularly have   to care. What I care about is: don’t build  the fucking superintelligence that gets us   killed. Let’s have the verification tech  in place, and let’s have the consequence. And the bloc here is useful to the extent that  it helps us impose consequence for defection.   So having, for example, Korea on board — South  Korea, to be clear — is important because Samsung   is there, because SK Hynix is there, right?  Having Taiwan on board is important because   of TSMC. So these are all helpful things. We  expect to be able to monitor what they’re up to,   so that our concern will be mirrored,  hopefully, by them. But beyond that,   let’s just make sure we don’t do the stupid thing.  And so I think that this is one sense in which—   I may be wrong in all kinds of fun and  interesting ways, but this worldview is   maybe a little bit more robust than the  one Dario is kind of putting forward. Robert Wright: OK, well, we end on a note of  agreement. Dario’s view is not necessarily   the optimal guiding light. But smart guy — I  think he’s sincere. I think he’s ideologically   sincere. I do not have the degree of cynicism  that I bring to bear on Sam Altman. Which isn’t   to say I want to appoint Dario— make him  in charge of world affairs. I wouldn’t— Jeremie Harris: Want to appoint anyone. Yeah. Robert Wright: Speak for yourself. I would want  to appoint myself, but I’m starting to think I   should give up on that career aspiration.  And you’re young — don’t give up on it. Jeremie Harris: I just have great skin. Robert Wright: Yeah, well, I wish  I did. Or were young. So anyway,   thanks. It’s been a great conversation.  There’s lots more you can talk about. So   I hope you’ll come back at some  point and we can keep going. Jeremie Harris: Yeah. Same here. Robert Wright: And again, people should  check out the podcast, and all your   reports at Gladstone AI. That’s the name, right? Jeremie Harris: Yeah.  aiendgame.com for the newsletter. Robert Wright: OK, good. So check it  out, folks, and we’ll see you next time. Jeremie Harris: Thank you.

transcript_segments.text: Rob Wiblin: Hey listeners. Today we’re  crossposting an interview with Jeremie Harris
from the NonZero podcast hosted by Robert Wright.  I had somehow not heard of Jeremie Harris already,
but I found this a super thought-provoking  conversation. Jeremie just had a lot of
ideas that were new to me, especially regarding  warning shots and the likely government response,
and also possible mistakes that have been made in  AI governance in the past. It’s all debatable, and
I’m sure not everyone will remember the history  the way that he does — I’m not sure that I quite
remember the history the way that he does — but  I think it’s provocative in a really useful way.
You might know the interviewer, Bob Wright  or Robert Wright, because he’s actually been
a guest on The 80,000 Hours Podcast before. He’s  also the author of a number of bestselling books,
perhaps most notably The Moral  Animal: Why We Are the Way We Are,
and he just published a new book about  the arrival of AGI called The God Test:
Artificial Intelligence and Our Coming  Cosmic Reckoning. If you’re somehow not
already convinced that the creation of  smarter-than-human machines is of cosmic
significance and will lead us to a new era in  the universe’s history, well, go read Bob’s book.
Bob now also does very regular interviews  about AI and AGI and superintelligence — he
interviewed Nick Bostrom a couple of weeks ago,  for instance. One of Bob’s strongest and most
distinctive views is that if the US and China  can’t set aside their differences and coordinate
to manage the arrival of superintelligence,  then we’ll probably just be toast as a species.
You’ll hear him make some of the case  for that perspective in this interview.
Anyway, I really appreciate Bob letting us  crosspost the conversation — especially the
second half, which was the highlight for  me, but has been completely stuck behind a
paywall until now. So thanks, Bob, and thanks,  Jeremie, and I hope you enjoy the crosspost.
Robert Wright: I’m Robert Wright, publisher  of the Nonzero newsletter. This is the
Nonzero podcast. I’m also author of  the recently published book on AI,
The God Test. Excerpts are  available at thegodtest.net.
And you are Jeremie Harris, and you  know a thing or two about AI. You are,
for starters, cohost of one of my  go-to AI podcasts, Last Week in AI,
cohosted with Andrey Kurenkov —  if that’s not too much mangling
of his name. And you are CEO and cofounder of  Gladstone AI, which in 2024 released a State
Department–commissioned report which I would  say, in retrospect, looks like it anticipated
some themes that are more prominent in the current  AI discourse. I’m sure you would say the same.
Jeremie Harris: I’m sure I would.
Robert Wright: I’m sure you would.  In fact, it may be that you have on
your podcast — I’m not sure, though.  But I was aware of it at the time,
and it was pretty much on my wavelength,  and that’s one reason I remember it.
For one thing, there was the recognition  that national security in the age of AI
cannot be secured through policy at  the national level alone. Ultimately,
you’re going to need what has lately been called  international coordination. And the report does
emphasise that — has a particular plan for getting  there. It emphasises the kinds of risks that we’ve
been hearing about lately: bioweapons, cyber —  and the phrase “loss of control” is in there,
something that has become more prominent in  the discourse since the Hugging Face incident.
So are you glad that regular  people have finally caught up
with your prescience? You  might not put it that way.
Jeremie Harris: Well, I’ll accept  the framing begrudgingly, but yeah,
I think it’s clear that right now the idea  of rogue AI is now sort of widely accepted,
because it has to — because  we’ve literally seen it.
So that report did come out in 2024, early 2024.  It was the product of research that started in
2023. Actually, the report itself was commissioned  by the State Department about a month before
ChatGPT — before the Eye of Sauron was on this  issue. Nobody in the US government was paying
attention to it, which meant that there was no  pressure to bureaucratise, let’s say, the output
of the work, the report itself. And so that’s  really the only reason that we were able to.
And so there was this sort of funny situation  that unfolded where basically we’re revealed to
be working on this thing that suddenly became of  massive public interest in the immediate aftermath
of ChatGPT. But it’s too late for the government  to— there’s no takebacks. And so off we go,
writing this report that the government now  knows will one day be public. And there’s
all this kind of political back-and-forth,  because the administration at that time — it
was Biden — did not want terms like AGI to  be used in this thing, because it seemed like
science fiction. They didn’t want terms like  “loss of control” to be included. And so we
had a pretty intense political fight behind the  scenes to make those things appear in the report.
We felt it was essential just because, as  you know, Silicon Valley has been talking
openly about artificial general intelligence  and superintelligence as being the end goal
of what they’re doing. I wouldn’t even call it  the worst-kept secret in Silicon Valley. It is
the open and stated primary objective of the  world’s most valuable companies at this point,
or many of them. And so anyway, we  just wanted that to become public.
I think one of the things in retrospect that  it kicked off was it was, to my understanding,
the first time that there were published in  kind of mainstream outlets sort of insider
whistleblower reports from the frontier  labs themselves. And at that time it was
a lot riskier. One guy took me aside after a  meeting at one of the frontier lab headquarters,
and he just gave me his phone, and his  hand was shaking. He was like, “Hey,
can you put your number in my phone?” And what  he told me at the time actually was, “Whatever
your recommendations in this report are going to  be, I would urge you to please be more ambitious.”
And later on, we met him literally at  a bar off site, just to kind of get the
rundown of what he meant by that. And  he was talking about nationalising the
frontier labs. This was 2023, he was  saying. We’re getting there, right?
So I think this kind of crazy world — these  sort of almost science fiction scenarios,
or what seemed like science fiction then — is  now starting to just become mundane reality. The
Overton window has shifted so much that I think  it’s time to reassess a lot of these proposals.
Robert Wright: Yeah. Let me say one thing in  anticipation of our conversation about where
you and I do and don’t overlap, because I think  this is what’s going to make this an interesting
conversation. As I’ve said, we both emphasise  the eventual need for something that I would call
international governance — you might or might not;  some people prefer other terms. But one difference
between us is I’ve heard you describe yourself as  a China hawk, and I’ve heard you talk like a China
hawk. I’ve heard me describe myself as definitely  not a China hawk. So it’ll be interesting to see
how we navigate some of these issues together,  and what we do and don’t agree on — on what’s
possible, first of all, and what’s necessary,  and what the implications of all this are.
But yeah, back to the discourse. It has been kind  of shocking. I mean, it’s funny: so you wrote this
report before some of this stuff happened. I put  this book of mine, The God Test, to bed before
the breakout — the OpenAI breakout — and the  trajectories we’re seeing now unfold are in
the book. We already had Moltbook and various—  and I talked about agents, and I talk about loss
of control. In fact, I have a chapter called “Hive  Minds and the Loss of Control.” Although I didn’t
anticipate the specifics of this kind of scenario.  So I’ve had this weird feeling of like, “Wait, so
I’m prescient? Oh, wait, no, it’s too late to be  pre—” It’s like— the discourse is moving so fast.
Robert Wright: And two things. First of all,  people in this realm have for some time been
saying, “Look, what’s it going to take to  get the world’s attention? I guess we’ll
need a warning shot” — by which they generally  mean some kind of high-casualty catastrophe.
In that sense, the news is good. The Overton  window’s moved a lot, very low body count.
There have been tragedies involving AI, but  so far as I know, nobody died at Hugging Face.
And so that’s all good. But I’m wondering  what you think in terms of, first of all,
what is the discourse still not  catching up to, in your view? And
secondly, do you think it’s still  going to take more kind of jolting
incidents of some kind or another to get  the discourse to where you want it to be?
Jeremie Harris: Yeah, I think these  are really complicated questions,
but I think, at least in my view,  they have a relatively simple answer.
The simple answer is there is still somehow  alpha in just taking scaling seriously.
So scaling is this idea — I think by  now it’s sort of a household idea,
but just in case it isn’t — this idea that  if you want to make an AI system smarter,
all you have to do, roughly speaking, is train  it at a larger scale, with more computing power
and more data. So you take this model,  this artificial brain, right? And again,
you use more AI processors, more of these chips,  built in a bigger AI data centre with more power
and so on. And now we’re at the scale where we’re  doing this with gigawatt scale. A gigawatt is
like a million homes’ worth of power, right? So  these are truly mammoth facilities and sites.
AI buildouts are responsible for the  lion’s share, if not basically all,
of US economic growth over the last  few quarters. So if you zoomed out,
you would see planet Earth is slowly  transforming itself — not so slowly,
even — into just a computing factory. And the  economy is sort of starting to reflect that,
the markets are starting to reflect that,  political pressures are starting to reflect
that. And yet the simple fact that scaling just  works is still something that, by believing it
more than others, you can still, I think, make  better predictions than the average person.
Back in 2020, the first time that  my cofounder and brother Ed and
I bet big on this was when we left our  company in 2020. There was a paper that
came out around that time. It was  the first big scaling laws paper.
Robert Wright: Was that a company you had  started? I’m just curious, what was it?
Jeremie Harris: Yeah, so it was an experiment.  And this— maybe, I don’t know if this goes to our
differences necessarily, but this was a hardcore  experiment in libertarian economic theory. So—
Robert Wright: Well, that would be one  difference, not necessarily related to the
China-hawkism issue. But yeah, I’m looking for  Milton Friedman on my bookshelf. Oh, not there.
Jeremie Harris: Yeah, yeah, absolutely. And to be  clear, as we age, our views become more nuanced.
But this was sort of a fun experiment in how far  could you take that? And so it had this notion
of income share agreements, where you might get  educated at some school or whatever, get some
training, and then the training could be monetised  by taking a percentage of your salary for a
certain period of time, so you don’t have to pay  upfront. And nominally, incentives are aligned in
that way. It actually kind of became the world’s  largest marketplace for income share agreements.
And we would do kind of peer to peer. So  if you wanted to break into, typically, AI
or data science, you’d work with a  mentor, and the mentor would say, “OK,
I’ll help you for free” — somebody who works  at Tesla or OpenAI — “in exchange for 3%,
5% of your first-year salary when you  get hired.” And so we had thousands and
thousands of these mentorships happening. It was  a really cool experiment, and we got some really
genuinely fascinating economic data from it  that is, I think, to this day quite unique.
But the scaling laws paper came out, and I  still remember I had a two-hour conversation—
Robert Wright: So this was Dario on  this paper? Yeah, when is this? And
this is establishing — arguing — that  yeah, all it takes is more compute,
more data. And that certainly has gotten us—  well, a lot of innovations have happened,
let’s face it. But that has partly driven what  we’ve seen. That was Dario’s name on that?
Jeremie Harris: Yep, that’s right. So Dario was  involved in all the early scaling research. In
fact, he was kind of the champion of scaling.  It’s often said of OpenAI that they are really
scale-pilled, and they are, but there are  a lot of ways in which Anthropic actually
is much more aggressively scale-pilled than  OpenAI, in different ways. And a lot of that
comes down to Dario. He was the earliest believer  in it, really, along with Ilya in a lot of ways.
Robert Wright: And he was at  OpenAI when they first showed
the benefits of scaling with the early ChatGPT.
Jeremie Harris: That’s right, yeah. And so if  you talk to the OpenAI people — so Jack Clark
will tell you GPT-2 is kind of the  moment that he went, “Whoa, whoa, whoa.”
And really, maybe it’s worth talking  about just what these things are scaling,
because it’s abstract to say you scale data,  you scale computing power or whatever. But
the actual thing that you’re scaling is  basically a text autocomplete engine.
And so all it does is it gets really good at  predicting the next word. It sounds stupid,
but text autocomplete ends up being, by  some weird freak of information theory,
this really important task. And you can  kind of understand why that’s the case.
If I give you a sentence like, “To counter a  rising China, the United States should blank,”
right? In order to fill in that blank — in order  to fill it in accurately — you need to know what
the United States is, what China is, what it means  for China to be ascendant. You need to know facts
about geopolitics, economics, all kinds of crap  that goes into just filling in that one next word.
And so this turns out to be a really powerful  way of teaching AI models just about the world
generally: facts about physics, about how to code,  about how to orient yourself in the world. And so—
Robert Wright: I mean, if I could add one thing.
Jeremie Harris: Yeah.
Robert Wright: You also need — if you’re going to  do that efficiently, and the process of training
forces the machine to do it efficiently — you need  a way of, for example, representing the meaning
of words. And I think it’s underappreciated—  something that the brain presumably does. I
think it’s underappreciated the extent to which  training is kind of the reverse engineering,
from language, of, I would say, some of the  cognitive functionality that in humans evolved
to help us deal with language. And then of course  there’s the subsequent so-called post-training,
where they do more than autocomplete: they teach  it to answer various kinds of questions and so on.
And I think the reverse engineering continues,
and this is why the ‘stochastic parrots’ people  are just not getting the power of what’s going
on. Without having to understand how the human  mind works, we’re kind of reverse engineering
the rough equivalent of it. And all you need  is the right kind of data and a lot of scale.
Jeremie Harris: Yeah, that’s right. And  the analogies and disanalogies are really
interesting here. There’s a sense in which it’s  really easy to get lost in the minutiae — the
Gary Marcus-ing of a lot of the conversation here  — where there’s always some fascinating reason
to believe that scaling will magically stop.  Perennially there is some fascinating argument:
we’re hitting a data wall, we’re hitting a  compute wall, we’re hitting an energy wall,
we’re hitting this wall, that wall.  Stochastic parrots, as you said, right?
